mainEntity.name: Why can’t I take the logarithm of zero or a negative number?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a positive base, bʸ is always positive, so no real y gives zero or a negative result. As x approaches 0 from above, log_b(x) heads to −∞ (a vertical asymptote). In the complex numbers, logs of negative numbers exist: ln(−x) = ln x + πi; this page shows that principal value for a negative argument.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between log, ln and log₂?

acceptedAnswer.text: They are logarithms in different bases: log is base 10 in most school and engineering contexts, ln is base e, and log₂ is base 2. In some programming languages and mathematics texts, “log” means the natural logarithm, so check the convention.

mainEntity.name: Why is the natural logarithm so important in calculus?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because d/dx ln x = 1/x with no extra constant. For any other base, d/dx log_b x = 1 ÷ (x ln b). The number e is the unique base for which the exponential function is its own derivative, which is why it appears in growth, decay and compound interest.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate a logarithm in a base my calculator lacks?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use change of base: log_b(x) = ln x ÷ ln b (or log₁₀ x ÷ log₁₀ b). For log₃ 500: ln 500 ÷ ln 3 = 6.2146 ÷ 1.0986 = 5.6568.
It is the inverse operation: the antilog of y in base b is bʸ. If log₁₀ x = 2.69897 then x = 10^2.69897 ≈ 500. Use the Antilog tab.
Because 1 raised to any power is 1, so 1ʸ can never equal any other number and log₁(x) would be undefined. Also, ln 1 = 0 would make the change-of-base formula divide by zero.
